fields.title: Custom Rubber Compound Development: What to Specify
fields.excerpt: Prepare a custom rubber compound request with operating conditions, material requirements, trial-process details and a measurable sample-approval plan.
fields.content:
Start a custom rubber compound project with a measurable specification: the contacting media, temperature cycle, mechanical duty, required properties and receiving manufacturing process. A useful development discussion connects those inputs to trial material, agreed tests and a clear sample-approval decision.

RubberQ brings Japanese formulation support together with compounding, molding and in-house testing in Fuzhou. The first step is to establish what the material must do in your component and how your team will judge the result.

Prepare the operating conditions before selecting a compound

A polymer name and hardness value give only part of the requirement. Describe the complete exposure sequence, including cleaning, storage and installation. Identify the dimensions and interfaces that control the component's function.

Information to shareDetails that make the review useful
Contact mediaFluid or gas identity, concentration, additives, contamination and cleaning agents
Temperature and timeNormal and peak conditions, duration, cycling and any cold-start requirement
Mechanical dutyCompression, movement, loading direction, contact surfaces and installation
Component definitionDrawing revision, critical dimensions, mating geometry and available reference parts
Material specificationExisting designation, hardness scale and tolerance, physical properties and acceptance methods
Manufacturing routeWhether you need molded parts or compound for your own process, including receiving-process requirements
Project demandTrial quantity, expected recurring demand, delivery destination and project stage

Agree what will be developed and who controls the specification

An existing specification may be the starting point. Where a requirement is still open, identify the function it needs to support and the evidence required to choose between candidates. Include the relevant customer requirements and the edition of any referenced standard.

ASTM D2000 provides a classification system for rubber materials. A designation should be considered together with the detailed requirements for the particular part. Include the complete callout and any additional test requirements in the project information.

Clarify specification ownership, confidentiality, permitted changes and approval responsibility. These arrangements help keep trial work and later production aligned as the drawing or material requirement develops.

Define the test basis with the candidate material

Agree the properties that matter to the application and the conditions under which they will be measured. Hardness, tensile behavior, aging, compression set or fluid exposure may form part of the discussion. Each requested result needs an identified material, sample, method and acceptance criterion.

A material test and a component test answer different questions. Include checks of fit, assembly and function where geometry or installation affects the result. For a bonded part, identify the insert and the loading direction as well as the elastomer requirements.

Evaluate trial material in the intended process

For finished parts, connect the trial to the drawing revision and the component inspection plan. Record what your team checks during sample approval and which results are needed before a recurring order.

For external compound supply, include the receiving process and intended finished-part requirements. Discuss trial-material form, packaging, storage information, batch identification and release documentation. Evaluate the trial in that process before agreeing the supply specification.

Connect the approved sample to repeat supply

Keep the approved drawing, material identification, test basis and change requirements together. RubberQ's ERP production records support traceability through manufacturing. Discuss the records and inspection information required for your orders, including how later specification changes will be communicated.

Development scope, tooling, trial charges and timing are agreed after the requirements have been reviewed. The project information above helps distinguish the material-development work from component tooling, testing and recurring production.

Send your compound-development requirements

Contact RubberQ with your drawing or application description, existing specification and expected quantity. Tell us whether you need formulation and compounding support, compound supply or a finished molded component so the technical discussion can begin with the right requirements.

fields.title: FKM vs FFKM: Compare Cost and Validation Requirements
fields.excerpt: Compare FKM and FFKM quotations using the same seal specification, candidate compounds, qualification work and your own maintenance-cost assumptions.
fields.content:
Evaluate an FKM-to-FFKM change by comparing the actual seal specification, operating conditions, validation effort and cost of a seal-related interruption. Request quotations for the same geometry and quantity, using identified candidate compounds. A fixed price multiple does not describe every material, part or order.

The useful purchasing question is which candidate can meet the documented requirements and what it takes to approve and maintain that choice. An upgrade should resolve a defined problem with an agreed test plan.

Describe the application before comparing quotations

Provide the drawing revision, inside diameter and cross-section or other critical dimensions, mating geometry and installation method. Identify the complete process exposure, including media, concentration, cleaning and temperature cycles. For equipment service, include the seal location and operating history.

When an existing seal has failed, retain photographs, unused reference parts and the conditions recorded around the failure. These inputs help distinguish a material question from damage during installation, a geometry issue or a change in operating conditions.

Keep material family and compound specification separate

FKM and FFKM are material families. The candidate for approval needs an identifiable formulation or grade, relevant data and a defined inspection basis. Ask which test conditions apply to the information being compared.

Review hardness, physical properties, exposure and functional checks as a connected requirement. Where purity, outgassing or plasma exposure matters, identify the relevant method and acceptance criteria for the particular process. A family name does not establish those results for an individual compound.

Request quotations on a common basis

Compare this itemKeep these details consistent or explain the difference
ComponentDrawing revision, dimensions, tolerances, surface requirements and quantity
MaterialCandidate identification, hardness requirement, supporting data and release tests
DevelopmentTrial material, sample quantities, tooling and responsibilities
QualificationMaterial tests, assembly checks, equipment trials and approval responsibility
SupplyOrder pattern, packaging, documentation, delivery destination and quotation validity
Change controlApproved specification, notification requirements and treatment of later changes

Separate one-time development or tooling charges from recurring part prices. Ask for the assumptions behind lead-time and supply discussions so procurement and engineering evaluate the same scope.

Compare the consequences of the decision

Use your own maintenance and operating records to estimate what a seal change could affect. Relevant items may include part consumption, planned replacement work, investigation time, downtime and the effort to qualify an alternative. Keep estimates separate from observed results.

A lower purchase price can be assessed alongside the work needed to approve and maintain the material. A higher purchase price also needs a clear technical reason. Compare both against your actual process, rather than assigning a universal cost ratio or service-life advantage to a polymer family.

Agree the validation before changing supply

Define what a sample must demonstrate and who accepts the result. Include fit and assembly checks with the material evaluation. Equipment-specific requirements may need a trial under representative operating conditions before the change is approved.

For an existing branded part, provide the reference together with the original specification and available dimensions. The reference helps identify the part being discussed; approval of a replacement depends on the application review and validation. See the FFKM replacement-seal review for the information needed to begin.

Prepare a comparison your team can approve

Bring the drawing, service conditions, current material reference, quantity and the problem your team needs to resolve. Discuss the FKM or FFKM requirement with RubberQ to define the candidate materials, sample work and quotation scope.

fields.title: O-Ring Visual Inspection: Specify Acceptance with ISO 3601-3
fields.excerpt: Prepare O-ring surface acceptance requirements, record imperfections and agree the inspection evidence needed for supplier review.
fields.content:
Agree the O-ring surface acceptance requirements before approving samples or production. State the applicable standard edition and quality grade, drawing requirements and inspection arrangement. A photograph can identify a concern, but acceptance needs the relevant criteria and a clear record of the part being assessed.

ISO 3601-3 addresses quality acceptance criteria and surface imperfections for O-rings. Use the applicable document to assess a specific imperfection; the standard's public summary does not provide the complete limits.

Put the acceptance basis on the purchasing specification

Give the supplier the O-ring dimensions, material specification, drawing revision and intended service. Include the standard edition and amendments required by the project, the selected quality grade and any additional customer requirements. Resolve differences between the purchase order, drawing and inspection instruction before production approval.

Keep dimensional tolerances, material properties and surface acceptance identifiable in the specification. A hardness value or material-family name cannot describe the permitted surface condition. Likewise, a dimensional inspection result does not record what was found on the surface.

Record what you see before deciding what it means

Identify the part, lot and quantity examined. Photograph the feature with a scale and enough context to show its location around the ring and across its cross-section. Record the viewing conditions and measurement method so the supplier can repeat the observation.

Observation to recordInformation useful for supplier review
Raised material or a visible mould lineLocation, measured size and whether the feature extends around the ring
Depression, opening or missing materialShape, dimensions, distribution and photographs from more than one angle
Mark, cut or local damageLocation, handling history and whether the part has been installed
Discolouration or surface depositPackaging, storage conditions, contact history and a retained sample

These descriptions help communicate the observation. Classifying the feature and deciding acceptance still require the applicable specification. Avoid assigning a pass or fail from a general defect photograph without the necessary dimensions and criteria.

Separate incoming condition from installation damage

State whether the O-ring was examined as received, after cleaning, after assembly or after service. Keep unused parts from the same lot available for comparison. Record any tools, lubricants or cleaning agents used and retain the packaging identification.

If leakage or damage appeared during operation, include the groove drawing, assembly sequence, media, pressure and temperature history. Surface appearance is one part of that investigation. See the seal failure investigation guide for the information needed to compare the component and its operating conditions.

Agree the inspection and reporting arrangement

Before ordering, discuss which characteristics will be checked, how samples will be selected, what equipment and viewing conditions will be used, and what report is required. Specify the handling of suspect parts and who can approve a deviation. Keep these arrangements connected to the drawing and purchase order.

When a concern arises, report the number examined and the number affected, together with lot identification and representative images. This gives the supplier a defined population to investigate and helps distinguish an isolated observation from a recurring issue.

Prepare a clear O-ring enquiry

Send the drawing, material requirement, standard references, quantity and intended application. If the enquiry concerns an existing part, add labelled photographs and the incoming or service history. RubberQ's precision seal enquiry can begin with these inputs, while the testing information helps frame the inspection and documentation discussion.

Contact RubberQ to discuss the part specification, sample requirements and acceptance information for your project.

fields.title: Rubber Part Quality Issues: Prepare an 8D Review
fields.excerpt: Organise part identification, affected quantities, samples and verification evidence for an 8D investigation of a rubber component quality issue.
fields.content:
When a rubber part shows a quality deviation, begin with the part identification, drawing requirement and observed condition. Preserve affected and unused samples, identify the quantities involved and agree how suspect material will be handled. These inputs support a useful investigation before a material or process change is proposed.

The 8D problem-solving approach provides a structure for organising the team, containing the issue, verifying causes and checking corrective action. For a purchased rubber component, the report needs to connect those activities to the actual part, lot, assembly and operating conditions.

Build an issue record the supplier can investigate

InputWhat to provide
Part identityPart number, drawing revision, material specification, order and lot markings
Observed conditionMeasured result or photographs, location on the part, and the requirement used for comparison
ExtentQuantity examined, quantity affected, locations and dates where the issue was found
HistoryStorage, cleaning, assembly and service conditions, including recent changes
Comparison samplesUnused parts from the same lot and available parts that performed as expected
Immediate needSuspect stock locations, assembly impact and the information needed for the next decision

Describe the observation precisely. “Leakage after assembly” and “surface damage found during incoming inspection” lead to different investigation paths. Keep a suspected cause separate from the condition that was actually measured or observed.

Use the 8D structure to make responsibilities clear

Agree the report format, responsible contacts and the updates the customer needs. The sequence below is a practical way to organise the discussion; the customer's required form and timing should be established for the project.

  1. Bring together the people who understand the component and its use.
  2. Define the problem and its affected population.
  3. Identify and check temporary containment.
  4. Investigate and verify the causes of occurrence and escape.
  5. Choose corrective actions and establish how to validate them.
  6. Implement the actions and check their effectiveness.
  7. Update relevant controls to reduce recurrence.
  8. Close the issue with an agreed record and team acknowledgement.

Connect the cause to the evidence

For a rubber seal, useful comparisons may include incoming dimensions and surface condition, material identification, assembly records and exposure history. A bonded part may also need photographs showing where separation occurred and the relevant substrate and process records.

A proposed material change should explain which requirement it addresses and what comparison will test that explanation. Changing a compound, a tool setting and an assembly method together can make the effect of each change difficult to assess. Define the comparison and retain the relevant samples and records.

Review why the issue occurred and why the applicable controls did not detect or prevent it. A replacement shipment may resolve an immediate supply need, while the investigation still requires evidence about the cause and the longer-term action.

Define what closes the issue

Agree the acceptance criteria, sample identification, test conditions and person responsible for confirming the result. Record which drawing, material or process revision applies to the evaluated parts. If the action changes an approved specification, establish the customer's approval requirements before further supply.

The closing record should state the action taken, the evidence reviewed and the follow-up needed under the agreed conditions. Separate a laboratory result, an assembly trial and observed service performance so procurement and engineering can assess each on its own basis.

Discuss a component concern with RubberQ

For an existing order or a new development enquiry, provide the part identity, requirement and available evidence. RubberQ's quality information, testing discussion and seal investigation guide can help organise the technical questions.

Contact RubberQ with the drawing, lot details and observed condition to begin the discussion.

fields.title: Rubber Batch Traceability: Records for Repeat Orders
fields.excerpt: Define the material, process, inspection and shipment records needed to support repeat rubber-part orders and investigate a lot-specific concern.
fields.content:
Traceability is the ability to connect a finished rubber part to the material, process, inspection, and shipment records that produced it. In a simple purchase, that may sound like paperwork. In a repeat production program, these records support comparisons between lots and the investigation of unexpected variation.

When a buyer asks why one lot feels different, why dimensions moved or why a part behaved differently after assembly, use the linked records to identify the material, process and inspection information available for comparison.

What a Traceable Rubber Lot Should Connect

A useful traceability system should not stop at a shipping label. It should connect several production layers:

  • Raw polymer and ingredient batches.
  • Compound recipe and mixing record.
  • Cure curve or rheometer data when required.
  • Molding machine, tool, shift, and process parameters.
  • Trimming or finishing method.
  • Inspection results and test reports.
  • Packing and shipment records.

The point is not to create a large document package for every order. The point is to make the record available when the application or buyer requirement calls for it.

Why Traceability Matters for Repeat Orders

Rubber materials are sensitive to small changes. Polymer supplier, filler lot, cure-package handling, mixing sequence, mold temperature, post-cure cycle, and storage condition can all influence final properties. For repeat orders, discuss how those variables are identified in the records and how the supplier retrieves the information associated with a shipment.

For EV, industrial equipment, semiconductor-related hardware, and Tier 2 supply programs, the risk is not only one bad part. The risk is losing confidence in whether the same material and process can be repeated over years.

ERP Records Are Useful Only When the Shop Floor Uses Them

When reviewing an ERP-based traceability system, ask how records are created and connected at receiving, weighing, mixing, molding, inspection, packing and shipment. Discuss the lot identifiers used, the records available and how the information can be retrieved for a particular order.

RubberQ uses ERP traceability alongside in-house compound preparation, molding and testing. During the enquiry, identify the records your program requires so the documentation scope can be discussed with the component and inspection requirements.

What Buyers Should Ask For

Buyer questionWhat it reveals
Can you trace this shipment to a compound batch?Whether material identity is controlled.
Can you reproduce the same compound next year?Whether recipe and process records are stable.
Which tests are connected to the lot?Whether inspection evidence follows the shipment.
How are changes approved?How material and process changes are reviewed and approved.

Use Records During Supplier Evaluation

Use the available records to assess how the supplier identifies material, controls the process and documents inspection. Where PPAP or another customer-specific submission is required, agree the applicable scope and the records to be included.

When a concern arises, connect the observed condition to the affected part, lot and order. Material and process records can help narrow the investigation; comparisons, inspection and relevant tests are still needed to establish the cause.

Discuss Record Requirements with RubberQ

RubberQ combines in-house compound preparation, molded-part production, inspection and testing. Include your drawing, material requirement, expected order pattern and documentation needs in the enquiry. These inputs help define the component, sample and record requirements for the program.

Review RubberQ quality capability, see factory operations, or send a project brief.

fields.title: Industrial Rubber Bellows: Material and Motion Review
fields.excerpt: Prepare movement, media, temperature and geometry requirements for industrial rubber bellows, then agree material and functional sample checks.
fields.content:
Industrial rubber bellows protect moving components from dust, fluids, metal chips, coolant spray, weather, and repeated flexing. They are used around shafts, linkages, sliding mechanisms, sensors, tool heads, and exposed moving assemblies. The material choice matters because a bellows does not simply seal a gap. It must move without cracking while resisting the surrounding environment.

A good bellows design starts with movement and exposure, not with a generic material name.

The Five Inputs That Drive Material Choice

  • Movement pattern. Axial compression, bending, torsion, and combined movement create different stress zones.
  • Cycle expectation. A cover moved a few times per day has different needs from a part flexed continuously.
  • Media exposure. Oil, coolant, grease, cleaning fluid, ozone, UV, and dust all influence compound choice.
  • Temperature range. Heat aging and low-temperature flexibility should be checked against actual service conditions.
  • Geometry. Wall thickness, fold radius, parting line, and mounting details determine where failure begins.

Common Material Families

Material familyTypical reason to consider it
EPDMWeather, ozone, water, and outdoor exposure.
NBROil and grease exposure in industrial equipment.
HNBRCombined heat, oil and movement requirements, subject to candidate-grade data.
VMQ siliconeWide temperature range and flexibility, when fluid exposure fits.
FKMHeat and specified fluid exposure where the candidate grade fits.

The table is only a starting point. A bellows compound may need customized hardness, filler package, cure system, and tear-strength balance to fit the part geometry.

Review Geometry Alongside Material

Review geometry alongside material when investigating a bellows failure. Fold-root shape, wall thickness, compression travel and mounting edges affect where movement and contact occur. Photographs and a comparison with unused parts can help identify the areas that need further evaluation.

Before tooling, buyers should share the full installed envelope, movement range, mounting method, and neighboring metal or plastic parts. That allows the supplier to review both compound and geometry together.

Testing That Helps

Protective bellows around robot joints and actuators

For a bellows protecting a robot joint or actuator, describe the complete movement and installed envelope, including combined motion where relevant. Identify mounting interfaces, nearby cables or components, and exposure to dust, fluids or cleaning. Use the full travel sequence when reviewing fold clearance and contact with surrounding parts.

Define the protection the assembly needs and how it will be evaluated. Keep the bellows drawing and material requirements connected to that trial. The robotics application discussion provides the project context; the movement and exposure specification remains specific to the component.

Useful validation depends on the application. For most industrial bellows projects, the buyer and supplier should discuss hardness, tensile strength, elongation, tear strength, heat aging, fluid resistance, and flex-cycle testing where practical. A simple material datasheet is not enough for a bellows that will move repeatedly in a dirty or hot environment.

RubberQ can help review drawings, recommend compound families, and produce samples for functional evaluation. When the project requires custom material support, our compounding and testing workflow can connect material design with molded-part behavior.

RFQ Checklist

  • Send the drawing plus installed movement range.
  • List oils, coolants, cleaning fluids, outdoor exposure, and temperature range.
  • Define target cycle expectation or service life.
  • Identify critical surfaces that cannot crack or rub through.
  • Ask the supplier to review fold geometry before tooling.

Define movement, exposure and acceptance requirements before approving a bellows material or tool. Discuss the drawing, installed envelope and sample evaluation together.

Review molded bellows requirements or send a bellows drawing for review.

fields.title: SPC for Rubber Parts: Reviewing Process Capability Data
fields.excerpt: Review rubber-part process capability with the drawing limits, measurement method, cavity and lot records, analysis assumptions and agreed action plan.
fields.content:
When evaluating a rubber-part supplier's process capability, ask which characteristic was measured, which specification limits applied and how the data were collected. A Cpk value is useful only with that context. Agree the evidence required for your part and production conditions before using an index to support approval.

NIST's process-capability guidance connects capability analysis with a stable process, specification limits and the distribution of measured results. A reported index describes the characteristic and data evaluated; it does not establish that every property of every part will conform.

Start with the drawing characteristic

Identify the part number, drawing revision and feature. State the units, specification limits and measurement conditions. For rubber components, record whether dimensions were measured after molding, after any post-cure or after the agreed conditioning period.

Separate a dimensional characteristic from a material property or assembly requirement. An O-ring cross-section study, a hardness result and an assembly leakage test answer different questions. Request the evidence relevant to each requirement that matters for your application.

Keep the production context with the results

Record to requestWhy it helps the review
Part and drawing revisionConnects measurements to the intended geometry and limits
Compound and production-lot identificationAllows material and process records to be compared
Tool and cavity identificationShows which production positions are represented
Dates, sequence and sampling planExplains the production interval and quantity evaluated
Measurement method and conditionsSupports comparisons between operators, equipment and sample states
Raw results and analysis methodAllows engineering and quality teams to review the reported estimate

For a multi-cavity tool, discuss how the study represents cavity differences. Keep material-lot changes, tool maintenance and relevant process changes identifiable in the record. Combining results without that context can make the source of variation difficult to investigate.

Ask how the index was estimated

Confirm that the analysis uses the correct drawing limits and explains the estimate of variation. Ask how process stability and the suitability of the statistical model were assessed. If predicted nonconforming quantities are reported, keep the assumptions with the prediction.

State the capability requirement agreed for the project and who accepts the study. The same numerical target does not automatically describe every feature, material test or customer program. A change in drawing limits or production conditions may also change the basis of the comparison.

Connect monitoring to an action plan

Discuss the response to a process signal or a measured nonconformance. The plan should identify who investigates, how affected material is identified and what evidence is needed before normal supply resumes. Process monitoring and inspection each have a role in the agreed control plan.

Use lot-linked records to distinguish an observed trend from a proposed explanation. A suspected material, tool or molding cause needs supporting investigation. Record the action and how its effectiveness will be evaluated.

Include the requirement in the supplier discussion

Send RubberQ the drawing, critical characteristics, expected order pattern and customer submission requirements. Discuss the measurement and reporting scope with the component, material and sample requirements. Where a PPAP submission is required, identify the applicable customer format and approval responsibilities.

See RubberQ's quality information, discuss the testing and measurement requirements, or send the part specification to begin the review.

fields.title: O-Ring Groove Design: Squeeze, Gland Fill and Tolerances
fields.excerpt: Review O-ring groove dimensions, squeeze and gland fill with the drawing tolerances, assembly geometry, operating media and sample-validation requirements.
fields.content:
Review an O-ring groove together with the seal cross-section, mating dimensions and operating conditions. Squeeze and gland fill describe different parts of that review: how much the cross-section is compressed and how much space the seal occupies. Neither number, on its own, establishes that an assembly will seal.

Begin with a drawing showing the assembled interface. Identify whether the seal is static or moving, how pressure acts, and which dimensions control the closed gap. A nominal O-ring size is only one input to that discussion.

Define the geometry before calculating squeeze

For a simple cross-section check, let d be the effective seal cross-section being evaluated and h the assembled gap in the direction of compression. The geometric calculation is:

Squeeze (%) = 100 × (d − h) / d

Use dimensions that describe the actual installation. Identify any installation stretch, the surfaces that establish the gap and the reference temperature. Keep this geometric check separate from the material response and the application's acceptance criteria.

Do not stop at nominal dimensions. Ask the design team to check the combinations of seal and mating-part tolerances that produce the smallest and largest compression. Record the drawing revisions used so later changes can be reviewed against the same basis.

Check available gland space separately

Gland fill compares the seal volume with the available gland volume:

Gland fill (%) = 100 × seal volume / available gland volume

The Parker O-Ring Handbook discusses squeeze and gland fill separately and identifies tolerances, swelling and thermal expansion as design considerations. Use the guidance applicable to the actual seal arrangement; a percentage taken from another application is not a finished design specification.

Prepare a drawing-review package

InputWhat to identify
Seal definitionInside diameter, cross-section, units, tolerances and material designation
Mating geometryGroove dimensions, closed gap, clearances, corners and surface requirements
AssemblyInstallation route, mating materials, fastening or closure method and permitted lubricant
ServiceFluid or gas, pressure history, temperature cycle and movement
AcceptanceLeakage criterion, test conditions, sample quantity and approval responsibility

Connect the calculation to sample evaluation

Agree how samples will be assembled and inspected before comparing candidate materials. Keep dimensional checks, installation observations and assembly-test results identifiable. Where the application includes movement, discuss the relevant operating cycle rather than relying only on a static closure check.

If a sample leaks, retain the seal and record the installation and test conditions before changing the groove or material. The investigation should distinguish an observed dimension or damage mark from a proposed cause. Changing several variables at once makes a comparison harder to interpret.

What should you send RubberQ?

Send the seal and mating-part drawings, current material specification, operating conditions and acceptance requirement. Include an existing sample or part reference where available and explain whether you are reviewing a new design or investigating an existing assembly.

Use the O-ring size guide to prepare dimensional information, review custom seal requirements, or send the groove and seal specification for a project discussion.

fields.title: Gasket Over-Compression: What to Check Before Tightening More
fields.excerpt: Investigate gasket compression with the closed gap, drawing tolerances, assembly method and service history before changing material or tightening further.
fields.content:
When a gasket leaks, tightening the assembly further should follow a review of the closed gap, gasket geometry and joint requirements. Record what was assembled and what changed before deciding whether the problem calls for a different material, a dimensional change or a revised installation procedure.

A flattened gasket is an observation to investigate. It does not, by itself, establish whether the original compression was excessive, the material changed during service or the joint moved under operating conditions.

Identify what controls the closed gap

Review the gasket drawing together with the mating parts. Identify whether stops, spacers, groove geometry or another feature limits closure. Record the gasket thickness and the dimensions of the closed assembly using an agreed measurement method.

If fasteners are involved, include the specified assembly sequence, lubricant and tightening method. Ask how joint closure is checked. Treat a fastening instruction and a measured gasket gap as different records; the review needs the information relevant to the actual joint.

Separate geometry, material and service observations

QuestionEvidence to collect
Was the intended gap achieved?Gasket and mating-part dimensions, tolerances, stops and assembly measurements
Where is the damage?Photographs showing edges, holes, corners, contact faces and orientation
Did the condition change in service?Operating time, fluid, temperature and pressure history, including cleaning
Was the same material installed?Compound identification, lot, drawing revision and available inspection records
Was the joint disturbed?Installation, maintenance, disassembly and any retightening history

Keep an unused gasket from the same lot where available. Record when and how the used part was removed and measured. Preserve both the observed condition and the original part identification so dimensional and material comparisons have a clear basis.

Do not transfer an O-ring rule to every gasket

The Parker O-Ring Handbook treats squeeze as a seal-design variable and distinguishes application arrangements. Its O-ring guidance should be read within that scope. A molded profile, flat gasket and O-ring can require different geometric reviews; agree the requirement for the actual component.

For a custom profile, show the section before and after assembly and identify the features intended to make contact. Ask which dimensions need control and how samples will be measured. Material hardness alone is not a complete drawing or installation specification.

Plan a comparison that answers the failure question

Write down the proposed change and the result it is intended to improve. If a new thickness, material or assembly setting is being considered, identify the comparison samples and the assembly conditions to keep consistent. Agree the leakage or functional test, operating exposure and inspection points.

A material compression-set result and an assembly leakage result describe different evaluations. Keep both with their test conditions rather than using one as a substitute for the other. If retained sealing force is important, include that requirement explicitly in the engineering discussion.

Prepare the next supplier discussion

Send RubberQ the gasket and joint drawings, material and lot identification, photographs and service history. State the current acceptance requirement and whether you need investigation support, a revised sample or a new component quotation.

See custom gasket requirements, organize evidence with the seal-failure guide, and discuss the relevant material and component tests.

fields.title: Rubber-to-Metal Bond Failure: Evidence for a Useful Investigation
fields.excerpt: Document where a bonded rubber part separated, preserve the mating surfaces and connect the observations with loading, service and test-method records.
fields.content:
Start a rubber-to-metal bond-failure investigation by documenting where separation occurred and preserving the affected surfaces. Record the component, material lot, insert and service history before cleaning or destructively testing the remaining samples. Visible separation helps frame the investigation; it does not establish the root cause on its own.

The useful question is how the observed damage relates to the part geometry, loading and manufacturing records. A result from a laboratory adhesion specimen also needs its method and conditions before it can be compared with another result or a failed component.

Record the location before interpreting it

Photograph the whole component and both sides of the separated region. Show orientation, loading direction and the position of the damage relative to the insert, corners and exposed edges. Include scale and identify any areas altered during removal.

Observation to recordInformation to retain
Rubber visible on an insertLocation, extent, thickness appearance and matching surface
Exposed insert surfacePhotographs before cleaning, surface condition and any visible coating
Crack or tear within the rubberApparent starting area, direction and surrounding geometry
Mixed separation across the partA location map rather than one label for the entire component
Damage created during removalThe extraction method and which observations may have been affected

Agree terminology with the teams reviewing the samples. Keep a description of what is visible separate from explanations such as contamination, surface preparation, cure conditions or overload. Those explanations need supporting records and comparison evidence.

Reconstruct the service and assembly history

Collect the drawing revision, elastomer identification, insert material and surface specification. Identify installation preload, loading direction, movement, frequency or cycle history where relevant. Include temperature, contacting media, cleaning and storage conditions.

Ask whether the problem appeared at incoming inspection, during assembly, in an agreed test or after service. Compare affected and unaffected components where available. Keep samples linked to lots and production dates rather than combining observations from unidentified parts.

Compare adhesion results on the same basis

ASTM D429 covers methods for rubber adhesion to rigid substrates. Its public scope distinguishes several specimen arrangements. Name the applicable method and edition, specimen geometry, loading arrangement and conditioning when requesting or reviewing a result.

For a component test, show how the part was held and loaded. Request the force record, any normalization used and the observed separation location. Do not compare figures from different geometries or loading methods as though the number alone described bond quality.

Turn the investigation into a controlled comparison

Agree which samples and records will test each proposed explanation. Identify any changed insert preparation, material, tooling or process condition. Keep the comparison and acceptance requirement specific enough that the engineering and quality teams can evaluate the result.

Static adhesion results, repeated-load performance and assembly function are separate requirements. Where the application needs dynamic validation, define that loading and acceptance plan explicitly rather than treating a peel result as proof of component life.

Send the component evidence

Contact RubberQ with drawings, photographs, lot identification and the operating or test history. State whether the request concerns a new rubber-to-metal component, an existing quality deviation or a comparison of candidate constructions. Discuss the test and reporting requirements alongside the sample plan.

fields.title: Compression Set in Seals: Reading Results and Investigating Failure
fields.excerpt: Review compression-set evidence with the specimen, exposure and recovery conditions, then connect it with the used seal, assembly and service history.
fields.content:
If a removed seal does not recover its earlier shape, document its condition and service history before assigning a cause. Compare the used part with the drawing, material identification and an unused sample where available. A compression-set test can support the material review, but it does not replace an investigation of the assembled seal.

Keep the question specific: are you reviewing a supplier's laboratory result, investigating leakage after service, or choosing an acceptance test for a new part? Each task needs a different set of records.

Read the test conditions with the result

ASTM D395 addresses rubber under compressive stress and includes different test arrangements. Its public guidance identifies compression-set tests as mainly relevant to static stressing conditions. Ask for the applicable method and edition rather than requesting an unqualified percentage.

Report informationQuestion for the review
Compound and specimen identityDoes the sample represent the specified material and relevant production state?
Method and specimen dimensionsWhat arrangement and measurements produced the reported result?
Compression and exposureWhat loading condition, temperature, duration and medium were used?
Recovery and final measurementWhen and under what conditions was the specimen measured after release?
Acceptance requirementWhich customer specification and limit apply to this result?

Compare candidate results on a common basis. If methods or conditions differ, identify the difference before ranking materials. A value without specimen and exposure details is an incomplete basis for a procurement decision.

Preserve the evidence from the actual seal

Photograph the seal in its installed orientation if possible and record how it was removed. Identify the material lot, drawing revision, installation date and operating interval. Include normal and peak temperatures, fluid composition, pressure events and cleaning exposures.

Measure the used and reference parts using an agreed approach and record the time since removal. Retain observations of cracks, cuts, swelling or displaced material separately from the recovery measurement. A description of the visible condition is more useful than labeling every flattened seal a material failure.

Review the assembly as well as the material

Request the mating-part geometry, closed gap, tolerances and installation method. Identify changes in the component, lubricant or operating conditions since approval. If leakage occurred, record the test or service conditions and the location observed before disassembly.

Keep dimensional recovery, retained force and leakage performance as distinct evaluation questions. If force retention is part of the application requirement, specify the relevant test discussion. If assembly function is the acceptance criterion, define the assembly test rather than inferring its result from a material value.

Agree what a revised sample must demonstrate

State the proposed material or geometry change and the comparison needed. Identify the exposure conditions, sample quantities, measurements and approval responsibility. Keep trial results connected to the compound and part revisions so a successful evaluation can become a clear repeat-order specification.

Ask how the comparison represents the intended duty. A static laboratory test does not establish performance for every movement, pressure cycle or service duration. Use the application's requirements to decide what additional component evaluation is needed.

Start with the part and service records

Send RubberQ the seal specification, available reports, photographs and operating history. Review seal and O-ring requirements, prepare the failure-investigation information, and discuss the material and component evaluation plan.

fields.title: Vacuum Seal Outgassing: Comparing Reports for Sensitive Equipment
fields.excerpt: Compare vacuum-seal outgassing evidence by test method, sample state, temperature and time, and keep it separate from leakage and particle requirements.
fields.content:
Choose a vacuum seal using outgassing evidence for the specific compound and sample condition. The report must identify what was measured, under which exposure, and how the result relates to your equipment. A polymer name, cleanroom classification or hardness value does not answer those questions.

For optical instruments and other contamination-sensitive equipment, begin with the affected function: an optical surface, process chemistry, pump-down requirement or another defined acceptance criterion. That determines which measurements are useful.

Identify the output before comparing the numbers

Outgassing results can describe different quantities. NASA's outgassing database description distinguishes total mass loss, collected volatile condensable material and water-vapour regain under a defined test procedure for spacecraft materials. These are separate outputs, not interchangeable names for one result.

Reported outputWhat to establish before comparison
Total mass loss, expressed as a percentageInitial sample mass, exposure and the basis of the percentage
Collected condensable materialCollection arrangement, temperatures, exposure and reported normalization
A mass or gas-release rateTime basis, units, exposed area or mass, temperature and measurement method
An assembly contamination or vacuum resultInstalled configuration, other materials present and the equipment acceptance criterion

A cumulative percentage from one test cannot be ranked directly against an area-normalized rate from another. The units describe different quantities. First establish the method and sample history; then decide whether the results answer the same engineering question.

Understand what a screening method establishes

ASTM E595 addresses total mass loss and collected volatile condensable material in a vacuum environment. NASA's published compilation applies this type of evidence to spacecraft-material selection. That context matters: a listed material result is not qualification of a different compound, a finished seal or an optical assembly.

If your project specifies an outgassing method, request its applicable edition and acceptance criteria. If it does not, define the contamination concern with the equipment owner before asking suppliers for a generic “low-outgassing” declaration. Keep the method's output separate from the equipment's functional approval.

Keep sample treatment visible

Record whether the sample was tested as supplied, after post-curing, after cleaning, after a bake-out or after another conditioning step. Identify the actual compound, lot and specimen geometry. Record storage and packaging history where they form part of the agreed preparation.

When comparing samples, use the same preparation basis or explain the difference. A result obtained after a defined treatment describes that sample state. Agree whether the production delivery will have that same state and which records are required to identify it.

Do not infer a universal post-curing or bake-out schedule from an unrelated material result. The proposed process, component dimensions and acceptance tests need to be reviewed together.

Separate outgassing, particles and sealing function

ISO 14644-1 classifies air cleanliness by airborne-particle concentration. That classification is a different measurement from a seal's release of volatile material. Ask for the evidence relevant to each requirement rather than using an air-cleanliness class as an outgassing certificate.

Keep assembly leakage and any gas-permeation requirement separately identified as well. A successful contamination screen does not establish the installed joint's leakage result. Conversely, a joint that passes a specified leak check still needs the contamination evaluation required by the equipment.

Build the comparison around your equipment

Share the seal and mating-part drawings, compound reference, vacuum and temperature cycle, contacting process media and any cleaning sequence. Identify which surfaces or functions are contamination-sensitive, what test results are required and who approves the equipment trial.

For a replacement, include the original part identification and the observed reason for the change. Keep fit, material evidence and equipment validation as separate approval questions. Review FFKM replacement requirements if that is the procurement route.

Send RubberQ the application and reporting requirements to discuss the candidate material and sample scope. The testing page provides a starting point for agreeing methods and records; the final evaluation should address the actual equipment conditions.

fields.title: Flash on Molded Rubber Parts: Specify the Acceptance Requirement
fields.excerpt: Define flash location, extension, thickness and inspection conditions on the part drawing so tooling, finishing and sample approval address the same requirement.
fields.content:
For a molded rubber part, specify where residual flash is permitted, what geometry is acceptable and how it will be inspected. “Flash-free” alone leaves those decisions unresolved. A useful drawing connects the requirement to sealing surfaces, assembly clearances, appearance and any particle-sensitive interface.

Flash is excess rubber associated with the molding process. The Parker O-Ring Handbook glossary describes it in relation to the mating mold surfaces and trimming. That definition helps identify the feature; acceptance still depends on the specified component and its use.

Describe the observed feature precisely

A thin projecting film, a ridge at a parting line, mismatched mold sections and a trimming cut should not be treated as one observation. Photograph the feature with scale and orientation. Identify whether you are specifying an acceptable finished part or investigating a deviation from an existing requirement.

For residual flash, distinguish its extension from the part and its thickness. Mark the location being measured and the direction of measurement. A single unlocated dimension can leave different teams inspecting different features.

Divide the part into functional zones

ZoneDrawing-review question
Sealing or contact faceWhere must contact be maintained, and what residual edge condition is permitted?
Assembly clearanceCould the finished edge interfere with insertion, motion or the mating part?
Exposed cosmetic surfaceWhat viewing conditions and reference samples define acceptable appearance?
Insert interfaceWhere are rubber coverage, exposed metal and any trim boundary defined?
Particle-sensitive regionWhat requirement applies to attached residue, loose material and handling after finishing?

Show permissible parting-line locations on the drawing where function requires control. Discuss tool design and part removal before fixing a blanket requirement for every surface. The agreed result should be inspectable on the finished component.

Use the standard that matches the part and feature

ISO 3302-1 concerns dimensional tolerances for specified rubber products; its public scope excludes precision toroidal sealing rings. ISO 3601-3 addresses quality acceptance and surface imperfections for O-rings within its scope.

A reference to a dimensional class is not a complete surface-acceptance instruction. State the applicable standard and edition, the relevant product scope, any specified grade and the drawing's additional requirements. Confirm the actual limits from the applicable document; do not infer a universal flash allowance from a standard's title.

Agree inspection before quoting “flash-free”

Define the measurement method, access to the feature, lighting or magnification where relevant, and the sampling arrangement. Keep approved reference samples identifiable by drawing revision. If an acceptance photograph is used, include scale and make clear which feature it illustrates.

Inspection also needs to recognize damage introduced during finishing. Agree how cuts, tears, displaced material or changes to a critical edge will be evaluated alongside the residual flash requirement. Removing a visible film is not the same as demonstrating that the finished part meets every drawing requirement.

Compare finishing routes against the same requirement

Review manual, mechanical or cryogenic finishing proposals with the actual material, geometry, inserts and quantity. Ask what sample evidence will establish the finished condition. A quoted route should be assessed by the agreed result rather than by the process name alone.

Tooling, access to trim areas, inspection effort and order pattern belong in the quotation discussion. Avoid attaching a fixed cost or cycle-time penalty to “flash-free” without the drawing and acceptance basis. State which surfaces need tighter control and why so the supplier can evaluate a specific scope.

Prepare the drawing and sample package

Send RubberQ the drawing with critical edge locations marked, the material specification, expected quantity and any reference samples. Include the intended inspection method and explain which edge conditions affect function or appearance.

Review rubber-molding requirements and the quality and documentation discussion together. For O-rings, identify the applicable surface-acceptance requirements separately from size and material selection.

fields.title: Dynamic Stiffness of Robot Rubber Mounts: Reading the Test Evidence
fields.excerpt: Specify robot-mount dynamic stiffness with preload, direction, amplitude, frequency and temperature, then distinguish component response from fatigue and system validation.
fields.content:
Specify a robot rubber mount's dynamic stiffness as a response under defined conditions, not as one material-hardness number. Identify the loading direction, installed preload, oscillation amplitude, frequency range, temperature and measurement arrangement. The resulting evidence must describe the component and the task it will perform.

For an actuator or joint assembly, distinguish supporting the static load, controlling relative motion, dissipating vibration and surviving repeated duty. These requirements can share a component, but they are not the same acceptance test.

Separate the curves you are reviewing

A slowly measured force-displacement curve describes the response over its stated loading path. A dynamic-stiffness plot describes a response to oscillating excitation under a stated test arrangement. Do not treat the two curves as interchangeable because they use the same specimen or compound name.

Read the axes and the reported definition. If stiffness is derived from force and displacement signals, identify the measurement locations, loading direction and how the signals were processed. Where a complex response is reported, retain the magnitude and phase or the reported component terms with their definitions.

NASA's research on elastomer stiffness and damping illustrates reporting complex stiffness against frequency for specified specimens and preloads. Its material results are not values for a different mount. The useful principle is to keep the response and the conditions together.

Make the operating point part of the specification

ConditionInformation needed for an interpretable comparison
Static operating pointPreload or installed deflection, orientation and available travel
ExcitationFrequency range, displacement or force amplitude, and whether amplitude is peak or peak-to-peak
DirectionCompression, shear, torsion or the defined combination, with axes marked
Temperature and historyTest temperature, conditioning, prior loading and any service exposure
Measurement arrangementFixture, attachment, sensor locations and the stiffness definition used
ResultUnits, frequency-dependent response, repeat measurements and acceptance limits

Keep compound, insert, geometry and lot identification with the data. If two candidate mounts differ in shape or attachment, the comparison is between those component configurations, not a measurement of polymer chemistry alone.

Choose a method for the actual measurement task

ISO 10846-1 provides principles for laboratory measurement of transfer properties of resilient elements and guidance for selecting the relevant part of that series. Use its guidance to define the relevant component measurement and discuss the required test scope with the laboratory. Robot-system acceptance remains part of the assembly-validation plan.

Agree the method and boundaries with the team using the data. Distinguish a measurement at the driven interface from a transfer-property measurement between interfaces. Report the arrangement clearly enough that a second team can understand what was constrained, excited and measured.

Keep stiffness, damping and durability as separate questions

Stiffness describes a force-displacement response under the stated definition. Damping concerns energy dissipation in the motion. A single stiffness value does not provide the complete damping response, and neither supplies a fatigue-life result.

A rubber-to-metal adhesion test addresses its own specimen and loading method. It cannot replace the mount's dynamic response or repeated-duty evaluation. If bond durability is critical, specify how the component will be loaded and inspected during the relevant duty sequence.

Define any post-test dimensional, bond, leakage or functional checks that the application needs. Retain the loading history and acceptance criteria with the result instead of reducing the qualification to an unqualified cycle count.

Connect the component result to the robot assembly

State what the assembly team wants to control: displacement at an interface, transmitted vibration, positioning behaviour or another measurable response. Component data should be evaluated in that system context, including the attachment and available motion. A mount report alone does not establish the robot's overall vibration or positioning performance.

Send RubberQ the component drawing and target response, insert specification, operating conditions and proposed validation plan. Review the requirements for rubber-to-metal components alongside the robotics application; agree the material, sample and reporting scope before comparing supply options.

fields.title: FFKM Seals for Plasma Equipment: Define the Evaluation Conditions
fields.excerpt: Evaluate FFKM plasma seals by compound, process exposure, seal location and measured outcomes, separating erosion, outgassing and assembly qualification.
fields.content:
Evaluate an FFKM seal against the actual plasma process and equipment position. Identify the compound, gas chemistry, exposure conditions, temperature and acceptance criteria before comparing erosion data. “Plasma-resistant FFKM” is not a complete specification for every chamber or cleaning sequence.

The procurement decision should connect three things: the material being supplied, the evidence for the relevant exposure and the qualification of the installed seal. A polymer-family description cannot establish that connection on its own.

Why the plasma conditions belong with the result

A 2024 study by Connolly and colleagues at the University of Illinois compared fluoroelastomer, FFKM and fluorosilicone under O2/Ar exposures separating full plasma, radicals and ions. Its published abstract reports different mass-loss and surface-change behaviour with those exposure conditions and the tested materials.

The study describes its O2/Ar specimens and exposure conditions. Compare candidates using evidence for the process and exact compound proposed for supply. Retain the material identity and exposure conditions with each measured outcome.

Describe the seal's process exposure

InputWhat to establish with the equipment team
Seal locationDrawing, equipment position, exposed surfaces and shielding or recess geometry
Process sequenceGas composition, processing and cleaning steps, exposure duration and cycles
Plasma arrangementDirect or remote exposure and available operating or diagnostic information
Temperature and pressureRelevant conditions at the seal, including transitions and excursions
Material stateSpecific compound, filler or formulation identification where available, lot and preparation
AcceptanceWhich measured changes matter and who approves the equipment trial

Separate a nominal equipment setting from a measurement or estimate at the seal. If a condition is unknown, identify it as a question for the process owner rather than substituting a generic material-temperature range.

Keep erosion, contamination and sealing results distinct

For an erosion comparison, ask whether the result is mass loss, a surface change, dimensional change or another output. Record exposure time, specimen geometry, preparation, normalization and measurement method. A rate without a time basis or exposed-area definition is incomplete comparison evidence.

Surface photographs and mass-change measurements can answer different questions. Agree how each result will be evaluated. If particles or extractable metals matter to the process, state those requirements and their test basis separately; an erosion result does not measure every contamination pathway.

Outgassing is another evaluation. NASA's outgassing description distinguishes mass loss and collected volatile condensable material for a defined vacuum test used in spacecraft-material selection. Those outputs should not be confused with plasma erosion, nor treated as semiconductor-equipment qualification.

Match the laboratory sample to the supply decision

Identify whether the sample represents the proposed compound and finished-part condition. Keep curing, post-treatment, cleaning, packaging and storage information with the sample record where relevant to the agreed evaluation. A result for an unidentified reference material is not a report for the ordered seal.

For repeated supply, agree the compound and drawing identification, required release information and how changes will be communicated. Discuss the project's documentation rather than assuming that every shipment includes every possible purity, particle or plasma test.

Validate the installed seal before changing supply

Material exposure data should be reviewed alongside fit, installation, compression geometry and the equipment's functional tests. Agree the trial configuration, inspection points, acceptance decision and any restrictions on interpreting the trial. Do not convert one laboratory comparison into a universal seal-life promise.

For an aftermarket replacement, include the original part reference and service history. Fit and performance require evaluation for the specific application; a reference to an existing brand or material is not OEM approval or proof of interchangeability.

Prepare a useful FFKM enquiry

Send RubberQ the seal drawing and process requirements, existing compound or part reference, expected quantity and the reports your team needs. Start with FFKM material requirements, review the semiconductor application context, or use the replacement-seal route for an existing equipment part.

fields.title: Compression Set vs Stress Relaxation: Two Different Seal Questions
fields.excerpt: Distinguish dimensional recovery after compression from force decay while compressed, and specify the method and conditions needed for each evaluation.
fields.content:
Compression set asks how much deformation remains after a specified compression and recovery procedure. Stress relaxation in compression asks how the force changes while a specified deformation is maintained. Both can matter to a seal, but a result for one does not supply the result for the other.

Choose the evaluation around the design question. If you need dimensional recovery after unloading, request the relevant compression-set evidence. If retained load over an exposure is important, define the force-decay requirement. Keep the assembly's functional acceptance test alongside these material or component measurements.

The measurement timeline is different

QuestionCompression setStress relaxation in compression
What is observed?Remaining deformation after the specified release and recoveryForce change while the specified deformation is maintained
What must accompany the value?Specimen, compression, exposure, recovery and measurement conditionsSpecimen, deformation, exposure, reference force and measurement times
What should not be inferred?The complete history of force in the loaded jointDimensional recovery after unloading or a universal leakage result

ASTM D395 addresses compression-set methods. ASTM D6147 addresses force decay in compression. Use the method and edition specified for the project; do not relabel a test because both involve a compressed specimen.

Read a force-retention percentage carefully

If a report expresses retained force as a percentage, identify the reference force and the point at which it was recorded. A simple normalization is the force at a stated time divided by the stated reference force, multiplied by one hundred. The result is only interpretable with those definitions and the loading history.

Request the force-time record where it is needed for the decision. Keep temperature changes, interruptions and measurement times visible. Two percentages based on different reference times or exposures are not a controlled material comparison.

Use comparable specimens and conditions

Identify the compound, cure and conditioning state, specimen geometry and production lot. Record the compression arrangement, test medium, temperature and duration. If results come from finished parts rather than standard specimens, retain the geometry and fixture description.

For candidates tested under different conditions, decide which differences need a matched trial. A family label such as FKM or EPDM cannot fill missing method information. Nor can an isolated percentage establish how a different section or joint will behave.

Connect the indicators to the seal design

A seal's installed geometry and service history remain relevant when reviewing either measurement. Bring the mating-part drawing, closed gap, tolerances, installation method and operating exposure into the evaluation. If leakage is the acceptance criterion, define that assembly test explicitly.

When investigating a used seal, preserve photographs, lot identification and the time since removal. Review the compression-set investigation guide for the evidence needed before assigning a cause. A flattened component is an observation; it is not a complete force-decay history or root-cause finding.

Specify the decision before requesting more tests

Tell RubberQ which question the report must answer and what acceptance requirement applies. Discuss whether the sample needs a material test, a component test or an assembly trial, and how the result will be connected to the approved compound and drawing.

Send the seal and evaluation requirements with existing reports. Use the testing discussion to agree methods, conditions and records before comparing numerical limits.

fields.title: Peel Test Reports for Bonded Rubber: Comparing Methods
fields.excerpt: Compare bonded-rubber peel reports using the specified method, specimen geometry, loading conditions, force record and separation location.
fields.content:
Compare two rubber-bond peel results only after checking the method, specimen geometry, loading arrangement and reported output. A 90-degree and a 180-degree description identify different arrangements; the angle alone does not provide a conversion between their results.

Start with the purpose of the comparison. Material development, process control and a finished-component investigation can require different specimens and acceptance criteria. Record which task the test is intended to support.

Name the method, not just the angle

ASTM D429 covers several methods for rubber adhesion to rigid substrates. Its public scope includes a 90-degree stripping arrangement among other specimen configurations. That does not mean every test labelled “peel” uses the same geometry or reports the same property.

Request the full method and edition, specimen preparation and any agreed departure from that method. For a production part, show how the specimen was obtained and held. Identify the rubber, substrate, surface specification and any preparation or conditioning relevant to the comparison.

Keep the force record and units together

Report fieldWhat to check
Force or normalized forceWhether the output is a force, force per specimen width or another defined quantity
Reported statisticWhether the value is a peak, average over a defined interval or another method-defined result
Specimen dimensionsThe actual width, rubber section, substrate and bonded region
LoadingAngle, rate, fixture and any movement or deformation affecting the arrangement
ConditioningTemperature, exposure, elapsed time and specimen preparation
SeparationLocation, extent, photographs and how mixed separation was described

Keep the trace or force record when it is needed to interpret a reported average or peak. Normalizing by width does not erase differences in geometry, loading or the region evaluated. A larger number from a different arrangement is not sufficient evidence of a better bond.

Report where separation occurred

Photograph both sides of the separated sample and identify rubber remaining on the substrate, exposed surfaces and any tear within the rubber. Map mixed regions rather than assigning a single label to the entire sample. Preserve the orientation and loading direction.

The rubber-to-metal failure investigation guide explains how those observations connect with component and service records. The observed location helps structure the investigation; proving a particular manufacturing or service cause requires additional evidence.

Design a comparison that answers one question

For candidate constructions, agree which variables remain the same and which change. Use the same method and acceptance basis where a direct comparison is required. If an existing customer method differs, define how each result will be used instead of creating an unsupported numerical conversion.

For a failed part, retain an unused comparison sample from the relevant lot where available. Identify whether extraction or cutting altered the surfaces. Keep the test result linked to the compound, insert and drawing revision.

Keep component duty separate from static adhesion

A static adhesion result does not supply a repeated-load or assembled-function result. Where the part will see oscillating load, temperature cycling or media exposure, specify that evaluation with its own specimen, sequence and acceptance criterion.

Send RubberQ the bonded-part drawing and existing reports to discuss the comparison. Review rubber-to-metal component requirements and agree the test and reporting scope before using a peel value in a supplier decision.

fields.title: ASTM D2000 for Rubber Parts: Use the Complete Material Callout
fields.excerpt: Use the full ASTM D2000 material designation, applicable edition and product-specific requirements when discussing compounds, test evidence and sample approval.
fields.content:
Send the complete ASTM D2000 material designation with the applicable edition and the part's detailed specification. A polymer name or a shortened callout can omit requirements that matter to material evaluation. Keep the classification, customer additions and proposed compound identification together throughout sampling and approval.

ASTM D2000 provides a material-classification framework. It is not a substitute for the drawing, application conditions or the customer's approval of the finished component.

Understand the classification's purpose

The ASTM D2000 public scope describes types based on resistance to heat aging and classes based on resistance to swelling in oil, together with additional requirements. It also gives the detailed specification for a particular product precedence where requirements conflict.

Those categories describe a test-based material requirement. They should not be read as a universal operating-temperature range or compatibility statement for every oil, coolant or chemical mixture. Use the complete designation and its applicable test requirements when evaluating a candidate.

Keep each part of the specification available

InformationWhy it belongs in the request
Standard and editionEstablishes which classification document the project uses
Complete material designationRetains the basic classification and all stated additional requirements
Drawing and customer additionsIdentifies product-specific properties, methods and limits
Application conditionsConnects the specification to the actual media, temperature and mechanical duty
Proposed compound identificationLinks the candidate material to sample and production records
Acceptance planStates which evidence and approvals are needed for the component

Do not remove suffixes or other characters to make the designation easier to quote. Ask the responsible engineering team to resolve an incomplete or ambiguous callout using the applicable document. A similar-looking designation should not silently replace the one on the controlled drawing.

Compare reports against requirements

Make a requirement-to-evidence list using the specified tests. For each result, identify the compound, specimen, preparation, method, exposure and acceptance limit. Distinguish information from a historical material sheet from results representing the agreed sample or production lot.

If two reports use different methods, media or exposure conditions, record the difference before drawing a conclusion. Passing one listed property does not establish the full designation, and a certificate heading does not replace the supporting scope.

Connect classification to the actual part

The material specification must be reviewed with the component geometry, dimensional requirements, installation and service. A material-test specimen and a finished gasket or bonded part are different evaluation objects. Identify the dimensional and functional checks needed alongside the material evidence.

For a non-standard requirement, discuss the property, method and acceptance limit explicitly. The custom compound-development guide provides the information needed to connect the application, receiving process and sample-approval plan.

Maintain the link through repeat orders

Retain the approved material designation, compound identification and drawing revision with the purchase specification. Agree how changes to material, process or testing will be reviewed and what records are needed for repeat supply.

Send RubberQ the full callout and drawing, including customer additions and expected quantity. Review the standards and specification requirements alongside formulation and compounding support so the discussion starts with the complete requirement.
